entry.name: Typewriter
entry.desc: The typewriter is a mechanical or electromechanical machine that prints characters on paper when a key is pressed, a type element striking an inked ribbon against the page. Its invention was incremental: Rasmus Malling-Hansen of Denmark invented the Hansen Writing Ball in 1865, and it went into commercial production in 1870 as the first typewriter sold. The first commercially successful model was patented in 1868 by Christopher Latham Sholes and others in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, and made by E. Remington and Sons from 1873 with the QWERTY layout, still the standard for English computer keyboards. Personal computers largely replaced typewriters after the 1980s.

row.label: Typewriter
row.contested: Historians estimate that some form of typewriter was invented 52 times: a British patent of 1714 granted to Henry Mill appears to describe a similar machine, and Pellegrino Turri built one for a blind friend between 1801 and 1808.

notes: Year: the article calls the invention incremental and lists many single early machines (Rampazetto 1575, Mill's 1714 patent 'appears to have been similar', Turri 1801-1808, Burt 1829). I dated the node to the Hansen Writing Ball (1865, first commercially sold, 1870) as the first machine of the line that went into use, and put Mill and Turri in contested. If the editor prefers Turri, the row would be year 1808, circa 1, date '1801–1808', place empty (the article gives none). built left empty: no earlier node is named as its basis.

entry.name: Phonograph
entry.desc: The phonograph is a device for the mechanical and analogue recording and reproduction of sound, in which a stylus traces a groove cut into a rotating cylinder or disc. Thomas Edison, working to play back recorded telegraph messages and to automate speech for the telephone, announced it in November 1877 and patented it in 1878; his first machines recorded on tinfoil wrapped round a grooved cylinder. Alexander Graham Bell's Volta Laboratory improved it in the 1880s with the graphophone and wax-coated cylinders, and in the 1890s Emile Berliner moved from cylinders to flat discs, naming his machine the gramophone. The disc record was the main commercial audio format for most of the 20th century.

row.label: Phonograph
row.contested: The phonautograph, patented in 1857 by Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville, recorded sound but could not play it back, and Charles Cros described a way of reproducing sound in a sealed letter of April 30, 1877, which he later had read to claim priority of conception.

notes: Place left empty: the article names no place for Edison's work (Menlo Park is not in it). Parents: the article says Edison conceived it as a byproduct of work on telegraph messages and the telephone.

entry.name: Lithography
entry.desc: Lithography is a planographic method of printing based on the immiscibility of oil and water: an image drawn with a greasy substance on smooth limestone or a metal plate takes the oily ink, while the wetted, etched surface around it repels it. The German author and actor Alois Senefelder invented it in the Electorate of Bavaria in 1796, and it was first used mostly for musical scores and maps. Godefroy Engelmann introduced multicolour printing, chromolithography, in 1837, and offset lithography, in which a rubber cylinder carries the ink from plate to paper, has printed most books and magazines since the 1960s.

notes: civ empty: the Electorate of Bavaria has no profile (the kingdom-of-bavaria entry begins in 1806), and Senefelder worked for no state. built empty: the article contrasts lithography with intaglio, woodblock and letterpress printing rather than deriving it from them.

entry.name: Morse code
entry.desc: Morse code is a method of telecommunication that encodes letters, numerals and punctuation as standard sequences of two signal durations, dots and dashes. Around 1837 the American artist Samuel Morse devised a code of numerals for the electrical telegraph he was developing with Joseph Henry and Alfred Vail; in 1840 Vail extended it to letters, giving the shortest signs to the commonest ones, and this code was first used in 1844. Friedrich Gerke's simpler Hamburg alphabet of 1848, adopted in Germany and Austria in 1851, led to the International Morse code of 1865, which also carried early radio communication from the 1890s.

row.label: Morse code
row.contested: The alphabet that carries Morse's name was Alfred Vail's, who extended Morse's numerals-only design in 1840, and most of the present international code comes from Friedrich Gerke's revision of 1848.

notes: Year: the article's 'Around 1837' for Morse's first code (numerals and a codebook), hence circa 1; the letter code dates from 1840 (Vail, Morristown, New Jersey). Place 'United States' since the article gives no town for Morse's 1837 work. civ empty: the article credits people, not a state.

entry.name: Braille
entry.desc: Braille is a tactile writing system used by blind and visually impaired people, in which characters are formed by six raised dots arranged in two columns of three, the braille cell. Louis Braille, a Frenchman who had lost his sight in a childhood accident, developed it in 1824 at the age of fifteen as an improvement on Charles Barbier's night writing, whose sets of 12 embossed dots encoded 36 sounds; Braille's cells stood for the letters of the French alphabet and added numerals and punctuation. He published the system, with musical notation, in 1829. Braille codes now exist for over 133 languages.

notes: Place left empty: the article says Braille was a Frenchman and the code used the French alphabet, but names no place (neither France nor Paris appears). Barbier's night writing is the precursor but is not on the tree. Type term/script, as a writing system.

entry.name: Radar
entry.desc: Radar is a system that uses radio waves to find the distance, direction and speed of objects such as aircraft, ships and weather formations; the United States Navy coined the name in 1940 from radio detection and ranging. In 1904 the German inventor Christian Hülsmeyer detected a ship in dense fog with his telemobiloscope, but German military officials rejected it. Pulsed radar was first shown in December 1934 by Robert M. Page at the Naval Research Laboratory, and in Britain Robert Watson-Watt's team built the Chain Home stations, operational from 1936, which helped the Royal Air Force win the Battle of Britain. The cavity magnetron made small sets possible.

row.label: Radar
row.contested: Radar was developed in secret by several countries before and during World War II; Heinrich Hertz had shown in 1886 that radio waves reflect from solid objects, and the first pulsed systems were shown in the United States in 1934 and in Germany and Great Britain in 1935.

notes: Year: Hülsmeyer's 1904 detection of a ship (patent April 1904, British patent for a full system the same year), which the article calls the first use of radio waves to detect distant metallic objects. Place: the article says only that he was German and tested it in Cologne and Rotterdam harbour (not saying where the 1904 demonstration was), so 'Germany'. Lane kept as communication per the brief, though weapons would also fit (Chain Home, air defence). civ empty: the German military rejected Hülsmeyer's device.

entry.name: Personal computer
entry.desc: A personal computer is a computer designed to be operated directly by one user, rather than shared by many through time-sharing like a minicomputer or mainframe. It was made possible by the integrated circuit and the microprocessor, the first single-chip one being the Intel 4004 of 1971; the Micral N, built from 1972, was the earliest commercial, non-kit microcomputer based on a microprocessor. The Altair 8800 of 1974 was the first commercially successful personal computer, the Commodore PET, Apple II and TRS-80 brought ready-assembled machines to a mass market in 1977, and the IBM Personal Computer of 1981 set the standard its compatibles followed.

row.label: Personal computer
row.contested: Which machine was the first personal computer is disputed: PC Magazine called IBM's SCAMP prototype of 1973 the world's first personal computer, the MCM/70 of 1973 is described as the first personal desktop microcomputer, and many consider the Altair 8800 of 1974 the first true one.

notes: Year: the Micral N (built from 1972), the earliest commercial non-kit microcomputer the article names; place left empty because the article gives none for it, and names no maker or inventor (people empty). Disputed firsts in contested. Parents: the article says the PC was made possible by semiconductor advances (integrated circuit, MOS transistor). There is no microprocessor node to link.

entry.name: Email
entry.desc: Email, or electronic mail, is a method of sending and receiving digital messages over a computer network, on a store-and-forward model in which servers accept, forward, deliver and store messages. Messaging between users of the same computer became possible with time-sharing in the early 1960s, with a notable implementation in MIT's CTSS project in 1965. In 1971 the first network mail was sent over the ARPANET, introducing addresses with the @ symbol for the user's system; the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol was implemented on the ARPANET in 1983, and after 1995 SMTP, POP3 and IMAP became the standard.

notes: Year: MIT's CTSS project in 1965, the first implementation the article names (messaging was possible 'after the advent of time-sharing in the early 1960s'). ARPANET (1969) cannot be a parent of a 1965 node, so the network mail of 1971 is in the desc only. Parent eniac as the plain dependence on the electronic computer; the editor may prefer none. The article names no person.

entry.name: Transatlantic telegraph cable
entry.desc: The transatlantic telegraph cables were undersea cables laid across the Atlantic Ocean for telegraph communication between Europe and the Americas. The Atlantic Telegraph Company, led by Cyrus West Field, laid the first from Valentia Island off Ireland to Trinity Bay, Newfoundland, and it carried its first messages on August 16, 1858, among them Queen Victoria's congratulations to President James Buchanan, but it failed after three weeks. Cables laid from the SS Great Eastern in 1865 and 1866 proved durable, and since 1866 the continents have been linked, so that a message could be answered on the same day rather than after weeks by ship.

row.label: Transatlantic cable
row.place: Valentia Island, Ireland, to Trinity Bay, Newfoundland
civ: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

notes: civ: the article says the British government gave a subsidy and loaned ships (HMS Agamemnon), and the United States Congress passed a subsidy and lent USS Niagara. People: Field (the company's leader), Bright (chief engineer) and Thomson (scientific adviser, later Lord Kelvin). Label shortened to fit 28 characters. The project began in 1854; the node is dated to the first working cable, 1858.

entry.name: Mercator projection
entry.desc: The Mercator projection is a way of drawing the globe on a flat map in which courses of constant compass bearing, rhumb lines, appear as straight lines, so that a chart serves sailors directly. Gerardus Mercator introduced it on his world map of 1569, printed from 18 copper plates he engraved himself, by increasing the degrees of latitude towards each pole as the parallels lengthen. He left no account of his method, and Edward Wright and others later showed how to calculate the latitude scale exactly. Acceptance was slow and came only with the French sea atlas Le Neptune Francois at the end of the seventeenth century; the projection is still the basis of navigation charts.

notes: Source article is 'Mercator 1569 world map'; the entry is the projection, introduced on that map. Place left empty: the article names no place where the map was made (only Rupelmonde, in a quotation, as Mercator's epithet). Parent magnetic-compass: the projection exists to straighten courses of constant compass bearing (rhumb lines) and the article discusses compass roses.

entry.name: Library of Ashurbanipal
entry.desc: The Library of Ashurbanipal is a collection of more than 30,000 clay tablets and fragments of the 7th century BCE, gathered at Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, by Ashurbanipal, king of the Neo-Assyrian Empire from 668 to 627 BCE. He had cities and centres of learning across Mesopotamia send him copies of their texts, sent scribes to collect them and took tablets as war loot; the texts, mostly Akkadian in cuneiform, were placed in rooms by subject and marked with coloured signs or their first words. The fire that destroyed Nineveh in 612 BCE baked the tablets, among them the Epic of Gilgamesh. Most are now in the British Museum.

row.label: Library of Ashurbanipal
row.contested: A similar library was found in 1849 in the palace of Sennacherib (705–681 BCE), and because the tablets of the two were mixed after reaching Europe, the contents of each can hardly be reconstructed.

notes: Year: the library is dated only by Ashurbanipal's reign (668–627 BCE) and '7th century BCE', so the row starts at his accession with circa 1. The article does not call it the first library; Sennacherib's earlier palace library is in contested. Type institution, subtype empty. civ the profile 'Assyrian Empire' (-2025..-609); the entry neo-assyrian-empire also exists.
